newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls after report of weak retail sales.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls after report of weak retail sales.

text.p: The dollar fell against major currencies Tuesday after a government report of lower retail sales in April convinced some investors the Federal Reserve would not raise interest rates again next week.

The Commerce Department said retail sales fell 0.3 percent in April, the largest drop since last June. The decline was widespread as consumers spent less on clothing, furniture, cars and other items. Sales in March also were revised lower.

Currency traders are keeping a close watch on economic data for clues as to whether Fed policy-makers will raise rates when they meet on Tuesday. The central bank raised short-term rates a quarter point on March 25. Higher rates tend to make dollar-based assets more attractive to investors.

"The market partly expected that the Fed might stay on hold," said Takanobu Igarashi, a senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd. in New York. "That's the reason for some dip in the dollar just after the retail sales report."
The dollar fell to 118.67 Japanese yen late in New York trading, from 119.45 yen late on Monday and to 1.6940 German marks from 1.7070.
It fell to 1.4375 Swiss francs from 1.4390 francs and to Canadian $1.3858 from C$1.3897. The British pound rose to $1.6332 from $1.6235.

The retail sales data will be followed by reports on producer prices on Wednesday and consumer prices on Thursday. The Fed is watching carefully to try to prevent robust economic growth from leading to a pickup in inflation.
Further hurting the dollar were remarks from senior Japanese officials that rippled through currency markets first in Asia and later in Europe and the United States.

Bank of Japan executive director Yutaka Yamaguchi told a parliamentary committee in Tokyo on Tuesday that a rise in Japan's long-term interest rates reflected investors' brighter outlook for the Japanese economy.
The remark, and higher rates in Japan, did not bode well for the dollar.

"Clearly, they're looking for a stronger Japanese economy later this year and higher rates will naturally follow and that should benefit the yen," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank Ltd. in New York.

Yamaguchi also said it was important for currency rates to stabilise at levels that reflected the economic fundamentals of the countries concerned. This sentiment was echoed by Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who said exchange rates were likely to settle at an appropriate level soon.

The pound rose after the Bank of England's inflation report said monetary policy needs to be tightened further or inflation will exceed the target level of 2.5 percent in coming years unless action was taken to slow economic growth.

The Bank of England's "independence itself is a good psychological boost for sterling and then comments like that that indicate they're going to be aggressive against inflation is also helping sterling," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Signet Bank.

Britain's new Labour government surprised investors last week by transferring responsibility for setting rates to the Bank of England. On the same day, short-term rates were raised to 6.25 percent from 6 percent.
Central banks often use higher rates in a bid to slow economic growth and ward off inflation.
